description: ​An ambitious team relying on data science, artificial intelligence, and fast software solutions (APIs/Data Tools) to tackle the space mapping and sky changes challenge. We focus on delivering a lightweight, smart web tool that retrieves NASA data and analyzes it in a simplified, direct manner without heavy applications or games.
summary:
Long space missions expose astronauts to harsh conditions like radiation and isolation, making it vital for them to monitor their own health without relying on constant contact with Earth or wearing uncomfortable medical devices all day. 
To solve this challenge, we developed a contactless health monitoring system that lets astronauts check their wellbeing quickly and easily. By simply looking at a computer camera, the system reads vital signs through facial changes and blinking patterns. It then instantly compares this data with space safety standards and displays the health status using simple color codes. If any issues are detected, the system provides immediate guidance and actions to help astronauts take care of themselves right away, or alert Earth if the situation requires urgent help.  
This project is essential because it empowers astronauts to independently manage their health during deep space exploration, overcoming communication delays and ensuring safety when medical help is far away.
details: AAstroGuard is a contactless predictive digital twin that lets astronauts assess their own health during long missions, where Mission Control can be up to 22 minutes away and wearing sensors around the clock is impractical. Using only the laptop webcam, it follows three steps: Gather → Evaluate → Act. First, it estimates heart rate from tiny colour changes in the skin of the forehead and cheeks (rPPG, using the POS algorithm, a 0.7–3 Hz Butterworth band-pass filter and an FFT peak search) and estimates fatigue from eye closure (PERCLOS) and blink-rate deviation over a 60-second window, while sleep, HRV, cabin CO₂ and solar particle events are entered through sliders and radiation dose and bone density are modelled from mission day and environment (ISS, Deep Space or Mars). Second, it evaluates these readings against NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight using a transparent rule engine (warning and critical thresholds across 8 indicators), cross-checked by a Decision Tree classifier (scikit-learn, trained on a 3,000-row simulated digital-twin dataset), with explainable AI that shows the decision path and each feature’s contribution, a 300-day risk forecast, and an interactive body twin whose brain, heart, lungs, skeleton and radiation hotspots turn green, yellow or red. Third, it acts by giving prioritised, immediate prescriptions for every flagged indicator (for example, moving to the storm shelter, adding resistive exercise load, resetting cabin lighting or checking the CO₂ scrubber) and, in a Critical state, raising a full-width alert and automatically sending a summary to Mission Control while telling the astronaut not to wait for the reply. The project offers several benefits: it removes the need for wearable sensors, which reduces crew discomfort, equipment mass and volume, and makes monitoring continuous and unobtrusive; it gives astronauts on-board autonomy, so they can assess their health and act immediately during communication delays instead of waiting up to 22 minutes or more for Earth; it shifts care from detection to prevention, because the mission forecast shows when a risk is likely to reach a warning or critical level so countermeasures can begin early; it builds trust and safety through explainable AI, colour-coded status and a rule-engine cross-check that let non-expert users understand why a result was reached and flag any disagreement for review; and it supports crew performance and mission success by catching fatigue, cardiovascular strain, bone loss, radiation exposure and cabin air problems before they become emergencies. Beyond space, the same low-cost, camera-only approach could support remote healthcare and the monitoring of isolated workers on Earth, such as polar stations, offshore platforms and rural clinics. It was built with Python, Streamlit, Plotly, OpenCV, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, pandas and joblib, developed with the help of AI tools (Gemini and Claude for ideation, coding and debugging, and Gemini also for generating images such as the astronaut body-twin visual) and Canva for design and for producing the demo video with Capcut for editing the video. Its creativity lies in replacing body-worn sensors with a camera and combining a medical rule engine with a machine-learning twin that checks itself, while accounting for crew comfort, lighting variability and safety, since it is decision support rather than a clinical device.
